“Alright Z. See ya soon.”

“Later” he said and hung up.

I wasn’t sure how he was going to get to the office before me but that was a slightly smaller mystery than these bridges. I got to my wife’s SUV and it suddenly dawned on me that if I took her truck, she and my daughter would be left at the recital without a ride home. I hung my head trying to figure out what to do when my phone rang. The display said ZARMACHECK. For once my partner was right on time.

“Heavy shit is hitting the fan” he said quickly. “I need you to give me your location so we can give you an immediate evac to Quantico.” While he wasn’t running, I could tell he was walking pretty quickly while he was talking to me.

I was dumbfounded. “Immediate evac? What the hell is going on Z?”

“Can’t say for sure right now but the boss man says you need to get your ass to the office. Now.” I heard a ping of an elevator in the background. “We’ve got a helo spooling up for you now at A.P. Hill. I took the phone from my ear and stared at the screen. I was so baffled by what I had heard I had to make sure I was talking to my partner. He had laid some heavy end-of-days crap on me and I felt like I was in a dream.

I was tired, but seeing my son John play the piano stroke an energy within me. His grandfather taught him well, well enough it was almost as if I was a kid again, coming back home to its gentle music. It's been a long while since I felt so ... light, like I didn't have a weight on my shoulder, like a girl with no worries, who read books while her father played piano.

When I was little, I always wanted be someone important doing important things. I studied well and graduated with double majors in criminal justice and international relations. I was so excited when I got the job at the Department of Homeland Security and after some cases, I became an investigative agent of national defense. I was finally respected by other (I think), and I sometimes allowed my self the vanity that I impressed people. My parents were proud of me, and I got to be part of the big picture.

My ... personal life was less stellar. I met Mr. Sutherland during one of those events of connections. After some sips of champagne and many polite dinners, he proposed. I didn't have a reason to refuse, and it was an ok marriage for the first few months. However, an ok marriage for few years made for a stagnant, and rather cold, one. My parents thought what we were missing was a kid, so I took a pregnancy leave. But Sutherland was almost always away from home. After pulling some strings and personal snooping, I found out about his affairs. I admit, I was a workaholic and wasn't exactly the warm, "loving" wife, but I had no obligation to Mr. Sutherland once that came to light. The fact that it was just so easy to find evidence, that he didn't even pretend when I approached him added insult to injury. It was the few times I ever lost my temper. I personally blamed pregnancy hormones.

We divorced. John was born. I went back to work.

I had trouble taking care of an infant, so I moved right next to my parents. So a decade passed. I had to be away for long periods of time, and my visits were becoming more brief after some terrorist acts on domestic grounds. There was always an air of tension at work. There were almost always sources indicating an incoming attack and some contradicting the notion. I never regretted being part of the big picture, but I never said I was invincible to stress. There was one thing I regret.

Dad sat next to me while I watched John on stage, playing a song no doubt composed by my father, a song that I was forever content to simply listen. I was proud of John, but did I have the right to? I didn't raise him, take care of him, or give him love from a mother; his grandparents did. I came back because often mom and dad would call me to remind me how long I was gone. I rarely came because of any other reason, including my own volition. I always worried that John would think that I didn't want to be with him. I wanted nothing less than to be home with him. But it was hard to relax being away from work while knowing (or not knowing) what was going on.

Me being here now was because a plan made a half-year prior, coinciding my scheduled off-day with the school performance. Another evidence to my guilt. My father smiled at me.

"He's better than me." Dad said.

"Yeah" I said without thinking. Dad chuckled and continued.

"If he wanted to, he should be getting lessons from a proper teacher. Being a pianist not a good way to sell labor, but it never hurt to learn." I simply nodded.

My phone vibrated. I flipped it open. I read the message.

By instinct, I sat up. I never put my car keys, my wallet, or my ID in my jacket pockets. My father put a hand on mine. I turned to face a pleading look.

"The song is almost over."

My throat briefly choked, but I suppressed it. I couldn't disguise my shaking. "I need to go." I couldn't hold my eyes up. "Do you think he'll understand?"

"Yes." My dad said with same unwavering conviction he gave whenever I asked that question. "John's like you in that way."

I gave a kiss to the cheek and walked fast to the exit. Before I pushed open the door, I looked back. I felt my feet frozen on the ground as the John was on the second last bar of his song. I thought of the victims I interviewed and interrogated. I thought of the ringing phones collected after the attacks and whom the calls must have been from.

In 6 seconds, I was at the last row of seats. In 14, I was on stage next to the piano. John looked shocked sitting on the piano seat, his hand lifted slightly away from the keys. I hugged him.

"I'm sorry for the show. It was wonderful." I whispered. "I'm sorry, I have to go. I love you."

John grabbed my clothes tightly. "Ok." His fist loosened as I let go. He turned back to the keys.

By the time I pushed open the exit door, John finished the song.
